newsitem.title: POLAND: Polish parliament seals health care reform.
newsitem.headline: Polish parliament seals health care reform.

text.p: Polish legislators on Thursday gave their final go-ahead on a bill reforming the country's inefficient communist-era health care service.

In a series of votes, the lower house of parliament approved most of the Senate's amendments to the bill which provides for the creation of health care funds to which all citizens would contribute 10 percent of their income on a tax-deductible basis.
The adoption of the Senate amendments, mostly minor, means the bill now goes to President Aleksander Kwasniewski who is likely to sign it into law.
Critics of the measure, from the opposition to the ruling left-wing coalition, say the new regulations are too bureaucratic and do not envisage enough decentralisation of the health care system.
The funds would cover the costs of medical consultations, basic drugs and regular hospital treatment after patients enter agreements with public health care units.
Patients would be allowed to choose their doctors and hospitals and thus funds allocated to a hospital or clinic would depend of the amount of service it provides.

Health Minister Ryszard Zochowski has said the regulations, to take effect in 1999, will introduce elements of the free market to the system, now centralised and directly financed from the budget, as hospitals and clinics will have to strive to attract patients.
The budget will continue to pay for medical schools and the construction of hospitals. It will also contribute premiums for those with no earnings.

Under the current system, health care should in theory be free for all Poles paying social security premiums. But the quality of medical service in state hospitals is often poor and patients face long waits for complicated surgery.
Many private clinics have been opened since the fall of communism in 1989, but few citizens can afford them in a country where an average gross monthly salary is about 1,000 zlotys ($350).
Underpaid doctors have been waging a protest campaign for wage rises and an increase in budget spending on health to six percent of gross domestic product from the current four percent.
